doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Goals and George Wein's Newport introduction
summary: His aim is to record more; he recounts getting George Wein to record a spoken intro for his Newport album.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Wow. Do you have goals? Musical goals?

There’s a great drummer named John Vidacovich in New Orleans that I played with a long time ago in the Astral Project, and we get to play together some, just a wonderful painter. And I heard him on the radio and the radio DJ said, “What’s your plans for the future?” And he goes, “Wow man, I hope to make my gig on time tonight.” So my goals are to — not be forgotten— record more. I just did, I told you I did this Newport record which I’ve been kind of editing on and working on. I’ll tell you a cool story. I thought how great would it be if George Wein did an intro for it, like he was on stage. So you know I went to his apartment, and he’s 93, and we visited for an hour talking, because I’m on the board of the New Orleans Jazz Festival which he started. And we were talking about things. And finally I realized, oh he’s getting tired now. I put a microphone in his hand, “George, you know what I need.” “Oh yeah.” And he hung his head for a minute. And I go oh shit, I’m overtaxing a 93-year-old man. He’s 96 now, or 95 now. And he finally raised his — “Many years ago I played on Bourbon Street with Red Norvo and Red Garland” — no, no, sorry. “Many years ago I played on Bourbon Street with Red Norvo and Barney Kessel. Across the street was Al Hirt, and a young man playing with Al Hirt was Ellis Marsalis. And he and I became fast friends. We hung out every night. Now New Orleans grows musicians, and one of Ellis’s protégés is a young man named David Torkanowsky. He played with Dianne Reeves and many great jazz artists and I’ve heard him play over the years and I said this man belongs at Newport. Ladies and gentlemen, David” he did that shit in one take. And I went oh my God what a gangster. He’s just the definition of the promoter, entrepreneur. So — and he was also a good pianist in the Dick Hyman school.
It’s not a bad school to be.

No. And he has this beautiful piano and this beautiful old pre-war New York apartment as you can imagine, it’s spacious and beautiful and expensive. And I said, “George, man, let me get an engineer and a rig over here, we’ll get a Anat Cohen over here and we’ll get a bass player and let me do a record.” And he goes ahh. I’m having trouble hearing you know, my time. And I said, “George your time was never that good to begin with bro, trust me.” Anyway he didn’t want to do it.
